o: Its fibres pass through the red nucleus before emerging into the interpeduncular fossa

The oculomotor nucleus lies in the periaqueductal grey at the level of the superior colliculus. Its fibres run ventrally through the tegmentum, passing through (and medial to) the red nucleus, and emerge on the medial side of the cerebral peduncle into the interpeduncular fossa.
This is why a midbrain lesion through the red nucleus (Benedikt's syndrome) combines a III palsy with contralateral tremor or ataxia. Do not confuse with IV, the only nerve to emerge dorsally.
Parasympathetic fibres reach the ciliary ganglion via the nerve to inferior oblique

Preganglionic fibres from the Edinger–Westphal nucleus travel in III, then in its inferior division, and leave it in the branch to inferior oblique (the motor root of the ciliary ganglion). They synapse in the ciliary ganglion; short ciliary nerves carry postganglionic fibres to sphincter pupillae and ciliaris.
Not via the nasociliary nerve: that gives the sensory root, which passes through the ganglion without synapse.
It passes through the superior orbital fissure outside the common tendinous ring

Both divisions of III enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure inside the common tendinous ring, together with the nasociliary nerve and VI.
The structures that pass outside (above) the ring are lacrimal, frontal and trochlear nerves (and the superior ophthalmic vein). A useful memory: everything that supplies the recti and the eye itself goes through the ring.
Pupillary fibres lie superficially in the nerve, so compression often dilates the pupil early

The pupillary (parasympathetic) fibres lie on the outer part of the nerve (dorsal, then medial, then inferior) and are supplied by vessels of the nerve sheath. External compression (posterior communicating aneurysm, uncal herniation) therefore affects them early and dilates the pupil.
By contrast, ischaemic infarction of the core of the trunk (diabetic III palsy) typically spares the pupil, because the superficial fibres keep their sheath blood supply.

questions.s: A complete right oculomotor nerve palsy produces:
o: Loss of the corneal reflex on the right

The corneal reflex has its afferent limb in V1 (nasociliary, long ciliary nerves) and its efferent limb in VII (orbicularis oculi). III plays no part, so the blink is preserved in a complete III palsy.
Do not confuse "eye closure" with "eye opening": III raises the lid (levator), VII closes it (orbicularis oculi).
Ptosis of the right upper eyelid

Levator palpebrae superioris is supplied by the superior division of III, so a complete palsy causes marked ptosis.
The ptosis is not quite complete because the superior tarsal muscle (Müller's), supplied by sympathetic fibres, is intact. In Horner's syndrome the ptosis is only partial for the opposite reason: levator is intact and only the tarsal muscle is lost.
Paralysis of the right lateral rectus

Lateral rectus is supplied by VI and is spared. Its unopposed action, together with superior oblique (IV), leaves the eye abducted and depressed: "down and out".
A lateral rectus palsy (VI) would instead leave the eye adducted, with diplopia on looking to the affected side.
A dilated right pupil unreactive to light

Parasympathetic fibres to sphincter pupillae run in III, so the pupil is dilated (unopposed sympathetic dilator pupillae) and does not constrict to light directly or consensually on that side.
The left eye's consensual response to light shone on the right is preserved, because the afferent limb (II) is intact. Accommodation is also lost (ciliaris).
Decussates in the superior medullary velum before emerging

All trochlear fibres cross dorsal to the aqueduct in the superior medullary velum before the nerve emerges just below the inferior colliculus. Each nucleus therefore supplies the contralateral superior oblique.
A nuclear or fascicular lesion before the decussation causes a contralateral superior oblique palsy; a lesion of the emerged nerve causes an ipsilateral palsy.
Has the longest intracranial course of any cranial nerve

IV is the thinnest cranial nerve and has the longest intracranial course, winding around the midbrain from its dorsal emergence, along the free edge of the tentorium, into the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus.
This long slender course makes it prone to stretch in closed head injury and at the tentorial edge. It is also the only nerve to emerge from the dorsum of the brainstem.
Enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure within the tendinous ring

IV enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure above (outside) the common tendinous ring, medial to the frontal nerve, and enters the upper surface of superior oblique.
Structures within the ring are the two divisions of III, nasociliary and VI. Because IV lies outside the ring, a retrobulbar block within the cone often leaves superior oblique working.
When paralysed causes diplopia worst on looking down and medially

Superior oblique is the main depressor of the adducted eye (it also intorts and abducts). Its paralysis gives vertical diplopia worst on looking down and in, as when reading or going downstairs.
Patients tilt the head away from the affected side to compensate for loss of intorsion. A lateral rectus palsy (VI) instead gives horizontal diplopia worst on looking to the affected side.
Its nucleus lies deep to the facial colliculus in the pons

The abducent nucleus lies in the floor of the fourth ventricle in the lower pons. Fibres of the facial nerve loop around it (the internal genu), raising the facial colliculus.
So a small lesion here usually damages both VI (or the gaze centre) and the looping VII fibres, giving an ipsilateral lower motor neurone facial palsy with the eye signs.
It passes beneath the petrosphenoidal ligament over the apex of the petrous temporal bone

VI runs up the clivus and passes over the apex of the petrous temporal bone beneath the petrosphenoidal (Gruber's) ligament in Dorello's canal. Here it is fixed and bent sharply.
That is why VI is the nerve most often affected as a "false localising sign" with raised intracranial pressure, and by petrous apex infection (Gradenigo's syndrome: VI palsy, retro-orbital pain, otorrhoea).
It runs within the cavernous sinus lateral to the internal carotid artery

Unlike III, IV, V1 and V2, which lie in the lateral wall, VI runs within the cavernous sinus itself, lateral to the internal carotid artery. It then enters the orbit through the tendinous ring.
Being free within the sinus, VI is usually the first nerve affected by a cavernous carotid aneurysm or a carotid–cavernous fistula.
A lesion of its nucleus causes isolated paralysis of lateral rectus

The abducent nucleus contains both motor neurones to lateral rectus and internuclear neurones that cross and ascend in the contralateral MLF to the medial rectus subnucleus of III. A nuclear lesion therefore causes a horizontal gaze palsy towards the side of the lesion.
Isolated lateral rectus paralysis comes from a lesion of the nerve, not the nucleus. A nuclear lesion often also catches the looping facial fibres.

questions.s: Branches of the nasociliary nerve include the:
o: Long ciliary nerves

The nasociliary nerve gives two long ciliary nerves, which carry sensation from the cornea and iris and carry sympathetic fibres to dilator pupillae. They are the afferent limb of the corneal reflex.
Do not confuse with the short ciliary nerves, which come from the ciliary ganglion and carry parasympathetic fibres (to sphincter pupillae and ciliaris) plus sensory and sympathetic fibres that pass through without synapse.
Posterior ethmoidal nerve

The nasociliary nerve gives the posterior ethmoidal nerve, which passes through the posterior ethmoidal foramen to supply the sphenoidal sinus and posterior ethmoidal air cells.
Its other branches are the communicating branch to the ciliary ganglion, the long ciliary nerves, the infratrochlear nerve and the anterior ethmoidal nerve (whose terminal part is the external nasal nerve).
Supratrochlear nerve

The supratrochlear nerve is a branch of the frontal nerve (with the supraorbital nerve), supplying the medial upper eyelid and forehead.
The nasociliary nerve gives the similarly named infratrochlear nerve, which supplies the medial canthus, lacrimal sac and side of the nose. "Supra" comes from frontal, "infra" from nasociliary.
External nasal nerve, the terminal part of the anterior ethmoidal

The anterior ethmoidal nerve passes through the anterior cranial fossa and nasal cavity and ends as the external nasal nerve, emerging between nasal bone and lateral nasal cartilage to supply the skin of the nasal tip.
Herpes zoster vesicles on the nasal tip (Hutchinson's sign) mean the nasociliary nerve is involved, which predicts ocular involvement because the same nerve supplies the cornea.

questions.s: Concerning the maxillary nerve and its branches:
o: It lies in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus below the ophthalmic nerve

In the cavernous sinus the maxillary nerve lies lowest in the lateral wall, below V1 (with III and IV above). It leaves the middle cranial fossa through foramen rotundum to reach the pterygopalatine fossa.
The order from above down in the lateral wall is III, IV, V1, V2. VI is not in the wall: it lies free in the sinus lateral to the internal carotid artery.
The posterior superior alveolar nerve arises in the pterygopalatine fossa

The posterior superior alveolar nerve arises from V2 in the pterygopalatine fossa, passes through the pterygomaxillary fissure and runs down the posterior (infratemporal) surface of the maxilla. It supplies the upper molar teeth, gums and maxillary sinus.
The middle and anterior superior alveolar nerves arise later, from the infraorbital nerve within the infraorbital canal.
The nasopalatine nerve supplies the mucosa behind the upper incisors

The nasopalatine nerve is a V2 branch that passes through the pterygopalatine ganglion without synapse, runs down and forward on the nasal septum, and passes through the incisive canal to supply the palatal mucosa behind the upper incisors.
The rest of the hard palate is supplied by the greater palatine nerve, which communicates with it. The soft palate is supplied by the lesser palatine nerves.
The infraorbital nerve supplies the skin of the upper eyelid

The infraorbital nerve supplies the lower eyelid, side of the nose, cheek and upper lip.
The upper eyelid is supplied by V1 (supraorbital, supratrochlear, lacrimal and infratrochlear branches). The dividing line is the palpebral fissure.
The nerve to medial pterygoid supplies tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini

The nerve to medial pterygoid arises from the main trunk of V3 and gives fibres that pass through the otic ganglion without synapse to supply tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini.
So all three muscles derived from the first arch that are supplied by this nerve (medial pterygoid and the two tensors) share one motor branch. Do not confuse with the anterior division, which supplies the other masticatory muscles.
The anterior division is mainly motor but gives one sensory branch, the buccal nerve

The anterior division of V3 is mainly motor (masseter, temporalis, lateral pterygoid) and gives one sensory branch, the buccal nerve. It passes between the two heads of lateral pterygoid to supply the skin and mucosa of the cheek.
Buccinator itself is supplied by the buccal branch of VII; the buccal nerve of V3 is purely sensory.
The auriculotemporal nerve usually splits around the middle meningeal artery

The auriculotemporal nerve arises from the posterior division of V3 by two roots that encircle the middle meningeal artery and then join.
It passes back behind the condyle of the mandible and carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibres (from the otic ganglion) to the parotid. Do not confuse with the chorda tympani, which joins the lingual nerve.
The mylohyoid nerve is a branch of the lingual nerve

The nerve to mylohyoid arises from the inferior alveolar nerve just before that nerve enters the mandibular foramen. It runs in the mylohyoid groove to supply mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric.
The lingual nerve gives no motor branches; it is sensory to the tongue and carries chorda tympani fibres. The posterior belly of digastric is supplied by VII.
Carries secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland

Secretomotor fibres to the parotid run in IX (tympanic branch), the lesser petrosal nerve, synapse in the otic ganglion and reach the gland via the auriculotemporal nerve.
The lingual nerve carries chorda tympani (VII) preganglionic fibres to the submandibular ganglion, for the submandibular and sublingual glands. Parotid = IX; submandibular and sublingual = VII.
Is joined by the chorda tympani about 2 cm below the skull base

The chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve from behind about 2 cm below the skull base, just above the lower border of lateral pterygoid.
It brings taste fibres for the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and preganglionic secretomotor fibres for the submandibular ganglion. Above this point the lingual nerve is purely V3 general sensation.
Supplies taste to the posterior third of the tongue

The posterior third of the tongue, including the vallate papillae, is supplied for both taste and general sensation by IX.
The lingual nerve supplies general sensation to the anterior two-thirds and carries the chorda tympani taste fibres for that part. The epiglottic region is supplied by the internal laryngeal branch of X.
Lies in contact with the periosteum below and behind the third molar

As it descends, the lingual nerve lies directly on the periosteum of the medial surface of the mandible just below and behind the third molar, where it may groove the bone.
It is therefore at risk in third molar extraction and lingual flap surgery, giving numbness and loss of taste over the anterior tongue.

questions.s: Concerning the intrapetrous course of the facial nerve:
o: The labyrinthine segment is the narrowest part of the facial canal

The labyrinthine segment, from the internal acoustic meatus to the geniculate ganglion, is the narrowest part of the facial canal.
The nerve almost fills the canal here, so oedema (as in Bell's palsy) compresses it most at this point. The tympanic and mastoid segments are wider.
The geniculate ganglion contains the cell bodies of taste fibres

The geniculate ganglion contains pseudounipolar sensory cell bodies, including those for taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (via chorda tympani) and the palate (via greater petrosal).
It contains no synapses for the parasympathetic fibres. These pass through to relay in the pterygopalatine and submandibular ganglia.
The nerve to stapedius arises in the tympanic (horizontal) segment

The nerve to stapedius arises from the mastoid (vertical, descending) segment in the posterior wall of the middle ear.
The tympanic (horizontal) segment gives no branches. The branches of the intrapetrous facial nerve in order are: greater petrosal (at the geniculate ganglion), nerve to stapedius, then chorda tympani (both from the mastoid segment).
The chorda tympani leaves the skull through the petrotympanic fissure

The chorda tympani arises from the mastoid segment, enters the middle ear, crosses the tympanic membrane medial to the handle of the malleus, and leaves through the petrotympanic fissure to join the lingual nerve.
Do not confuse with the greater petrosal nerve, which leaves the petrous bone through its own hiatus on the anterior surface into the middle cranial fossa.

questions.s: A lesion of the facial nerve within the facial canal distal to the geniculate ganglion but proximal to the nerve to stapedius would cause:
o: Ipsilateral paralysis of the muscles of facial expression

All motor branches to the muscles of facial expression arise after the nerve leaves the stylomastoid foramen, so a lesion anywhere in the canal paralyses the whole ipsilateral face (lower motor neurone pattern, forehead included).
A supranuclear (upper motor neurone) lesion would instead spare the forehead.
Loss of lacrimation on the affected side

The greater petrosal nerve leaves at the geniculate ganglion, proximal to this lesion, so its fibres to the pterygopalatine ganglion and lacrimal gland are intact and tear production is normal.
Lacrimation is lost only with a lesion at or proximal to the geniculate ganglion. Testing tears is a classic way to localise a facial nerve lesion.
Normal hearing with no hyperacusis

The lesion is proximal to the nerve to stapedius, so stapedius is paralysed. Sounds seem abnormally loud (hyperacusis) because stapedius can no longer damp the stapes.
Hearing as such is not lost, because VIII is not involved. A lesion distal to the nerve to stapedius would spare it.
Normal taste over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue

The chorda tympani arises distal to the nerve to stapedius, so it is also cut off and taste over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is lost on that side.
Taste would be spared only by a lesion distal to the origin of the chorda tympani (for example at the stylomastoid foramen).
It gives branches to the posterior belly of digastric and to stylohyoid

Just after leaving the stylomastoid foramen the facial nerve gives the posterior auricular nerve and branches to the posterior belly of digastric and to stylohyoid.
These second-arch muscles are supplied by VII. The anterior belly of digastric is first arch and is supplied by V3 (nerve to mylohyoid).
In the parotid it lies superficial to the retromandibular vein

Within the parotid the structures lie, from superficial to deep, as facial nerve, retromandibular vein, external carotid artery.
The nerve and its plexus divide the gland into "superficial" and "deep" parts surgically; the vein is a useful landmark deep to it in parotidectomy.
The marginal mandibular branch may loop below the lower border of the mandible

The marginal mandibular branch may run up to 2 cm below the lower border of the mandible, behind the facial artery, before turning up across it.
This matters for submandibular incisions, which are placed well below the mandible to avoid weakness of depressor anguli oris (a crooked smile).
It supplies the buccinator through the buccal branch of the mandibular nerve

Buccinator is a muscle of facial expression supplied by the buccal branch of the facial nerve.
The buccal nerve from V3 shares the name but is purely sensory to the cheek skin and mucosa; it pierces buccinator without supplying it.

questions.s: With a unilateral upper motor neurone lesion of the facial pathway (for example capsular infarct):
o: The forehead is relatively spared

The part of the facial nucleus supplying the upper face (frontalis, upper orbicularis oculi) receives corticonuclear fibres from both hemispheres. A unilateral upper motor neurone lesion therefore leaves the forehead moving.
Forehead sparing is the key sign that separates an upper motor neurone lesion from a lower motor neurone (Bell's type) palsy, where the whole face is weak.
The lower face on the side opposite the lesion is paralysed

The part of the nucleus supplying the lower face receives mainly crossed input. A capsular lesion therefore weakens the lower face on the side opposite the lesion.
The face is weak on the same side as the hemiparesis, because both corticonuclear and corticospinal fibres cross.
Emotional facial movement may be preserved

Emotional (mimetic) facial movement is driven by limbic and extrapyramidal pathways separate from the voluntary corticonuclear fibres, so a spontaneous smile may be symmetrical despite voluntary weakness.
The reverse dissociation (voluntary movement preserved, emotional lost) occurs with some thalamic or frontal lesions.
Taste is lost on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue

Taste fibres are sensory and run in the chorda tympani to the nucleus of the tractus solitarius. They are not part of the corticonuclear motor pathway, so a capsular infarct does not abolish taste.
Taste is lost with lesions of the facial nerve proximal to the chorda tympani, not with upper motor neurone lesions.
It supplies only one muscle, stylopharyngeus

IX is the nerve of the third pharyngeal arch, and stylopharyngeus is the only muscle derived from that arch and the only muscle IX supplies.
The other pharyngeal and palatal muscles are supplied by X via the pharyngeal plexus (except tensor veli palatini, by V3).
It provides general and taste sensation to the posterior third of the tongue including the vallate papillae

IX gives both general sensation and taste to the posterior third of the tongue, including the vallate papillae, even though these lie just in front of the sulcus terminalis.
The anterior two-thirds is supplied by the lingual nerve (general) and chorda tympani (taste); the region near the epiglottis by the internal laryngeal nerve (X).
Its tympanic branch carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibres destined for the parotid gland

The tympanic branch (Jacobson's nerve) enters the middle ear, forms the tympanic plexus on the promontory, and continues as the lesser petrosal nerve to the otic ganglion. Postganglionic fibres reach the parotid via the auriculotemporal nerve.
This is the parotid pathway; the chorda tympani (VII) supplies the submandibular and sublingual glands instead.
It passes between the internal jugular vein and internal carotid artery deep to the styloid process to reach the tongue

After leaving the jugular foramen IX passes forward between the internal and external carotid arteries, winds around the lateral side of stylopharyngeus, and enters the pharynx between the superior and middle constrictors to reach the tongue.
Lying between the internal jugular vein and internal carotid artery is the course of X (in the carotid sheath) and of XII early in the neck, not IX.

questions.s: Regarding the laryngeal branches of the vagus:
o: The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane

The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal artery. It is sensory (and secretomotor) to the mucosa above the vocal folds, including the piriform fossa.
It is the afferent limb of the cough reflex above the cords; a foreign body in the piriform fossa can damage it.
The external laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid and is closely related to the superior thyroid artery

The external laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid (and part of the inferior constrictor) and runs with the superior thyroid artery towards the upper pole of the thyroid.
It is at risk when the superior thyroid pedicle is ligated, so the artery is tied close to the gland. Damage lowers voice pitch and power, because cricothyroid tenses the cords.
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the left subclavian artery

The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the arch of the aorta, beside the ligamentum arteriosum, a sixth-arch derivative.
It is the right nerve that hooks under the right subclavian artery, because the right sixth-arch artery disappears. The longer left nerve is more often involved in thoracic disease (aortic aneurysm, lung cancer).
The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies sensation below the vocal folds

The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies sensation to the laryngeal mucosa below the vocal folds, and all the intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid.
Above the folds sensation is from the internal laryngeal nerve. The vocal folds themselves mark the dividing line.

questions.s: The pharyngeal branch of the vagus supplies:
o: Palatoglossus

Palatoglossus is supplied by the pharyngeal branch of X through the pharyngeal plexus. It is the only "glossus" muscle not supplied by XII, because it is really a palatal muscle.
Remember the pattern: all palatal muscles are X except tensor veli palatini (V3); all tongue muscles are XII except palatoglossus (X).
Tensor veli palatini

Tensor veli palatini is supplied by V3, via the nerve to medial pterygoid, with fibres passing through the otic ganglion without synapse.
It is a first-arch muscle, like tensor tympani. Every other palatal muscle (levator veli palatini, palatoglossus, palatopharyngeus, musculus uvulae) is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (X).
Styloglossus

Styloglossus is an extrinsic tongue muscle supplied by XII.
The vagus supplies palatoglossus but not the other extrinsic tongue muscles (genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus), all of which are XII.
Stylopharyngeus

Stylopharyngeus is supplied by IX, the only muscle that nerve supplies (third arch).
All the other pharyngeal muscles (the constrictors, palatopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus) are supplied by X through the pharyngeal plexus. Stylopharyngeus is the classic exception.

questions.s: Concerning the vagus nerve in the neck and thorax:
o: It lies in the carotid sheath posterior to and between the internal jugular vein and carotid artery

In the carotid sheath the vagus lies posteriorly, in the groove between the internal jugular vein (lateral) and the internal and then common carotid artery (medial).
The ansa cervicalis lies on or in the front of the sheath, and the sympathetic trunk lies behind it, outside the sheath, on the prevertebral fascia.
Its auricular branch supplies part of the external acoustic meatus

The auricular branch (Arnold's nerve) supplies the skin of the posterior wall of the external acoustic meatus and the outer surface of the tympanic membrane.
That is why syringing or touching the meatus can provoke coughing or even vomiting or syncope (vagal reflexes). The rest of the meatus and the drum are supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve (V3).
The right vagus passes anterior to the root of the right lung

Both vagi pass behind the roots of the lungs, contributing to the posterior pulmonary plexuses, then go on to the oesophageal plexus.
It is the phrenic nerves that pass in front of the lung roots. "Phrenic in front, vagus behind" is the rule for the hilum on both sides.
The left vagus crosses the arch of the aorta deep to the left phrenic nerve

On the left side of the aortic arch the left phrenic nerve lies anterior and the left vagus lies posterior (deep), with the left superior intercostal vein crossing the arch between them. The vagus then gives the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, which hooks under the arch.
On the right, the vagus lies on the trachea and passes behind the right lung root.
Arises from the anterior grey horn cells of the upper five cervical segments

The spinal accessory nucleus is a column of anterior horn cells in the upper five (C1 to about C5) cervical segments. Its rootlets emerge between the anterior and posterior roots and ascend through the foramen magnum.
The cranial root (from the nucleus ambiguus) is really part of the vagus and joins it outside the skull.
Leaves the skull through the jugular foramen

The spinal accessory nerve enters the skull through the foramen magnum and leaves through the jugular foramen, in the same dural sheath as the vagus.
The jugular foramen also transmits IX (in front, in its own sheath), the internal jugular vein (behind) and the inferior petrosal sinus. A jugular foramen lesion (Vernet's syndrome) affects IX, X and XI together.
Crosses the posterior triangle deep to the prevertebral fascia

XI crosses the posterior triangle superficially, embedded in or just deep to the investing layer of deep cervical fascia that forms the roof, lying on levator scapulae.
The prevertebral fascia forms the floor of the triangle and covers the brachial plexus and phrenic nerve. Because XI is so superficial, it is easily cut in lymph node biopsy, causing trapezius weakness and shoulder drop.
Supplies sternocleidomastoid and then emerges about halfway down its posterior border

XI enters the deep surface of sternocleidomastoid, supplies it, and emerges about halfway down its posterior border. It then crosses the posterior triangle to trapezius.
The lesser occipital nerve hooks around XI at the posterior border, a useful landmark (Erb's point lies just below). Trapezius also gets proprioceptive fibres from C3 and C4.
Hooks around the occipital artery as it descends

As XII descends from the hypoglossal canal it hooks forward around the origin of the sternocleidomastoid branch of the occipital artery.
It then runs forward above the greater horn of the hyoid towards the tongue. This hook is a landmark for finding the nerve in carotid surgery.
Crosses lateral to the internal and external carotid arteries and the loop of the lingual artery

XII crosses superficially (lateral) to the internal carotid, external carotid and the loop of the lingual artery as it runs forward.
It is at risk in carotid endarterectomy, especially with a high bifurcation. The structures it crosses all lie deep to it.
Lies on the lateral surface of hyoglossus below the submandibular duct

On the lateral surface of hyoglossus the order from above down is lingual nerve, submandibular duct, hypoglossal nerve (with its venae comitantes).
The lingual artery runs deep to hyoglossus, which separates it from XII. The lingual nerve loops around the duct here: lateral, then below, then medial.
Carries fibres of C1 that form the superior root of the ansa cervicalis and supply thyrohyoid and geniohyoid

C1 fibres join XII near the skull base and travel with it. Some leave as the superior root of the ansa cervicalis (descendens hypoglossi); others leave as the nerves to thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.
These fibres are not from the hypoglossal nucleus. XII itself supplies only tongue muscles. The inferior root of the ansa is C2 and C3.

questions.s: Following a right lower motor neurone hypoglossal nerve lesion:
o: The protruded tongue deviates to the right

Each genioglossus protrudes the tongue towards the opposite side. With the right paralysed, the left genioglossus is unopposed and pushes the tip towards the weak right side.
The tongue points to the side of a lower motor neurone lesion. An upper motor neurone lesion (corticonuclear) causes much milder deviation, usually towards the side of the hemiplegia.
The right side of the tongue becomes wasted and fasciculates

A lower motor neurone lesion denervates the right half of the tongue, which wastes, wrinkles and shows fasciculation.
These signs (wasting, fasciculation, flaccidity) distinguish lower motor neurone lesions (nucleus or nerve) from upper motor neurone lesions, where the tongue is not wasted.
Taste over the right anterior two-thirds is lost

XII is purely motor to the tongue muscles. Taste over the anterior two-thirds travels in the chorda tympani (VII), and over the posterior third in IX.
General sensation is also unaffected: anterior two-thirds via the lingual nerve (V3), posterior third via IX.
Palatoglossus is paralysed

Palatoglossus is supplied by the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus, so it is spared in a XII lesion.
Palatoglossus is the only extrinsic tongue muscle not supplied by XII.
The otic ganglion receives preganglionic fibres from the inferior salivary nucleus

Preganglionic fibres from the inferior salivary nucleus run in IX, its tympanic branch, the tympanic plexus and the lesser petrosal nerve to synapse in the otic ganglion. Postganglionic fibres reach the parotid via the auriculotemporal nerve.
The superior salivary nucleus (VII) instead supplies the pterygopalatine and submandibular ganglia.
The pterygopalatine ganglion receives preganglionic fibres via the greater petrosal nerve

Preganglionic fibres from the superior salivary (lacrimatory) nucleus run in the nervus intermedius and greater petrosal nerve, which joins the deep petrosal nerve to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal, reaching the ganglion.
These fibres drive lacrimal, nasal, palatal and pharyngeal glands. Do not confuse with the lesser petrosal (IX, to the otic ganglion).
The submandibular ganglion sends postganglionic fibres to the parotid gland

The submandibular ganglion receives chorda tympani fibres via the lingual nerve and sends postganglionic fibres to the submandibular and sublingual glands.
The parotid is supplied from the otic ganglion via the auriculotemporal nerve (the IX pathway).
Sympathetic fibres synapse in the ciliary ganglion

Only parasympathetic fibres (from III via the Edinger–Westphal nucleus) synapse in the ciliary ganglion. Sympathetic fibres from the internal carotid plexus, which have already synapsed in the superior cervical ganglion, pass through without synapse, as do sensory fibres from nasociliary.
The same applies to all four cranial parasympathetic ganglia: only parasympathetic fibres relay there.
It lies just below the foramen ovale, medial to the mandibular nerve

The otic ganglion lies in the infratemporal fossa just below the foramen ovale, on the medial side of the mandibular nerve and lateral to tensor veli palatini.
The ganglion is closely attached to the nerve to medial pterygoid, which passes through it.
Its sympathetic root comes from the plexus on the middle meningeal artery

Postganglionic sympathetic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion reach the otic ganglion from the plexus around the middle meningeal artery and pass through it without synapse.
They join the parasympathetic fibres to the parotid (vasomotor). Each cranial ganglion gets its sympathetic root from the nearest arterial plexus.
Its sensory root is from the auriculotemporal nerve

The auriculotemporal nerve provides the sensory connection of the otic ganglion, and the same nerve carries its postganglionic secretomotor fibres onward to the parotid.
Sensory fibres pass through the ganglion without synapse, as in all the cranial parasympathetic ganglia.
It has a motor root from the nerve to medial pterygoid

Unusually, the otic ganglion has a somatic motor connection: fibres from the nerve to medial pterygoid pass through it without synapse to supply tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini.
None of the other three ganglia (ciliary, pterygopalatine, submandibular) has a motor root of this kind.
Sends secretomotor fibres to the lacrimal gland via the zygomatic and lacrimal nerves

Postganglionic secretomotor fibres from the pterygopalatine ganglion join V2, travel in its zygomatic branch, then pass by a communicating branch to the lacrimal nerve (V1) to reach the lacrimal gland.
The preganglionic fibres came from the superior salivary nucleus via the greater petrosal nerve. A lesion of the greater petrosal nerve causes a dry eye.
Receives sympathetic fibres via the deep petrosal nerve

The deep petrosal nerve carries postganglionic sympathetic fibres from the internal carotid plexus. It joins the greater petrosal nerve to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal (Vidian nerve), which enters the ganglion.
The sympathetic fibres pass through without synapse. "Greater = parasympathetic, deep = sympathetic" is the way to keep them apart.
Is suspended from the maxillary nerve in the pterygopalatine fossa

The pterygopalatine ganglion lies in the pterygopalatine fossa, suspended from V2 by two short ganglionic branches.
Sensory fibres of V2 pass through these branches and the ganglion without synapse to form the palatine, nasal and pharyngeal branches. The ganglion is the largest of the cranial parasympathetic ganglia.
Contains the cell bodies of taste fibres from the palate

Taste fibres from the palate run with the palatine nerves, pass through the ganglion without synapse, and reach the greater petrosal nerve. Their cell bodies are in the geniculate ganglion of VII.
Only parasympathetic fibres synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion; sensory cell bodies are never in an autonomic ganglion.
It is surrounded by dura, arachnoid and pia, with an extension of the subarachnoid space

The optic nerve is an outgrowth of the brain, so it is ensheathed by dura, arachnoid and pia, and the subarachnoid space extends along it to the back of the globe.
Raised intracranial pressure is therefore transmitted to the nerve head, obstructing axoplasmic flow and venous return and causing papilloedema. The central retinal vein crosses this space.
The central retinal artery enters the nerve on its inferomedial aspect about 1 cm behind the globe

The central retinal artery, a branch of the ophthalmic artery, pierces the dural sheath on the inferomedial aspect of the nerve about 1 cm behind the globe and runs in the nerve to the optic disc.
It is an end artery; occlusion causes sudden painless monocular blindness with a cherry-red spot at the macula.
Its intraorbital part is shorter than the distance from the optic canal to the back of the globe

The intraorbital part of the nerve (about 25 mm) is longer than the straight distance from the optic canal to the back of the globe. It follows a slightly sinuous course, which allows free eye movement and some proptosis without stretching.
If it were shorter, eye movements would tug on the nerve.
Its fibres are axons of the retinal ganglion cells

The optic nerve fibres are the axons of retinal ganglion cells. Developmentally the nerve is a CNS tract, myelinated by oligodendrocytes, not Schwann cells.
As a result it does not regenerate after division, and it is affected by CNS demyelination (optic neuritis in multiple sclerosis).
The olfactory nerves pass through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb

About 20 bundles of olfactory nerve fibres (unmyelinated axons of the receptor cells) pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid, each with a sleeve of meninges, to end in the olfactory bulb.
A fracture of the cribriform plate can tear them (anosmia) and allow CSF rhinorrhoea through these sleeves.
Olfactory impulses relay in the thalamus before reaching the primary olfactory cortex

Olfaction is the only sense whose impulses reach the primary cortex (piriform and periamygdaloid cortex, uncus) without relaying in the thalamus.
Every other sensory pathway (vision, hearing, taste, general sensation) relays in the thalamus first. Some olfactory connections later reach the thalamus (mediodorsal nucleus) and orbitofrontal cortex, but that is not the primary pathway.
The lateral olfactory stria passes to the uncus and amygdala

The olfactory tract divides into medial and lateral striae. The lateral stria ends in the piriform cortex, the uncus and the amygdala: the primary olfactory cortex.
That is why an uncal lesion can cause olfactory hallucinations ("uncinate fits"). The medial stria passes to the septal area and the anterior commissure.
The olfactory receptor cells are not replaced in adult life

Olfactory receptor neurones are unusual among neurones in being continually replaced throughout adult life from basal cells of the olfactory epithelium.
This turnover helps recovery from minor damage to the receptors, but not from shearing of the fibres at the cribriform plate.

questions.s: Concerning the vestibulocochlear nerve and pathways:
o: The cochlear nuclei lie on the inferior cerebellar peduncle

The dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei lie on the dorsal and lateral aspects of the inferior cerebellar peduncle at the pontomedullary junction. All fibres of the cochlear nerve end in them.
A lesion of the cochlear nuclei or the nerve causes ipsilateral deafness, unlike a lesion higher in the pathway.
The lateral lemniscus ascends to the inferior colliculus

The lateral lemniscus carries auditory fibres from the cochlear nuclei, trapezoid body and superior olivary nuclei up to the inferior colliculus. From there the inferior brachium passes to the medial geniculate body, which projects to the auditory cortex.
Do not confuse with the medial lemniscus, which carries dorsal column sensation to the thalamus.
A unilateral lesion of the lateral lemniscus causes total deafness in the contralateral ear

Above the cochlear nuclei the auditory pathway is bilateral: fibres cross in the trapezoid body and at higher levels, so each lateral lemniscus carries input from both ears. A unilateral lesion causes at most reduced hearing (mainly in the opposite ear), not complete deafness.
Complete unilateral deafness means a lesion of the cochlea, the nerve or the cochlear nuclei.
The spiral ganglion lies in the modiolus of the cochlea

The bipolar cell bodies of the cochlear nerve form the spiral ganglion, which lies in the spiral canal of the modiolus, the central bony pillar of the cochlea.
The vestibular nerve has its own ganglion (Scarpa's) in the internal acoustic meatus.
The afferent limb of the corneal reflex is the ophthalmic nerve

The afferent limb of the corneal reflex is the ophthalmic nerve, via the long ciliary branches of the nasociliary nerve, to the trigeminal sensory nuclei. The efferent limb is VII to orbicularis oculi on both sides.
Testing it checks V1. Its early loss is a sign of a cerebellopontine angle tumour compressing the trigeminal root.
The efferent limb of the jaw jerk is the facial nerve

Both limbs of the jaw jerk are in V. The afferent fibres come from muscle spindles in masseter, with cell bodies in the mesencephalic nucleus, and the efferent fibres are from the trigeminal motor nucleus.
A brisk jaw jerk indicates an upper motor neurone lesion above the pons (for example pseudobulbar palsy). VII has no role.
The efferent limb of the gag reflex is the hypoglossal nerve

The efferent limb of the gag reflex is X (with some IX for stylopharyngeus), arising from the nucleus ambiguus, to the pharyngeal and palatal muscles. The afferent limb is mainly IX.
XII moves the tongue and plays no part in the gag reflex.
The efferent limb of the pupillary light reflex is the trochlear nerve

The efferent limb of the pupillary light reflex is III: preganglionic fibres from the Edinger–Westphal nucleus synapse in the ciliary ganglion and short ciliary nerves supply sphincter pupillae.
IV supplies only superior oblique and plays no part in pupil control. The afferent limb is II, relaying in the pretectal nuclei.

questions.t: Cranial nerves at the skull base
questions.s: Which nerves lie in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus?
o: Abducent nerve

VI lies within the cavernous sinus itself, lateral to the internal carotid artery, not in the lateral wall.
Being inside the sinus, VI is often the first nerve affected by a cavernous carotid aneurysm or fistula.
Oculomotor nerve

III is the highest nerve in the lateral wall, above IV, then V1 and V2 lowest.
It enters the roof of the sinus between the free and attached edges of the tentorium (the oculomotor triangle) before descending into the wall.
Greater petrosal nerve

The greater petrosal nerve leaves the hiatus on the anterior surface of the petrous bone, runs under the trigeminal ganglion to foramen lacerum, and joins the deep petrosal to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal. It is not in the cavernous sinus wall.
The nerves in the wall are III, IV, V1 and V2.
Maxillary nerve

V2 lies in the lowest part of the lateral wall before leaving through foramen rotundum.
V3 does not pass through the cavernous sinus; it leaves the trigeminal ganglion straight down through foramen ovale.

questions.t: Cranial nerves in the posterior fossa
o: The facial nerve lies anterosuperior to the vestibulocochlear nerve

At the cerebellopontine angle and in the internal acoustic meatus, the facial nerve and nervus intermedius lie anterosuperior to VIII.
In the fundus of the meatus the facial nerve occupies the anterosuperior quadrant, the cochlear nerve the anteroinferior, and the two vestibular nerves the posterior quadrants. Vestibular schwannomas stretch VII over their surface.
The anterior inferior cerebellar artery often loops near the internal acoustic meatus

The anterior inferior cerebellar artery runs back on the inferior surface of the cerebellum and often forms a loop at or into the internal acoustic meatus. The labyrinthine artery usually arises from it (sometimes directly from the basilar artery).
This loop is relevant in cerebellopontine angle surgery and in neurovascular compression.
A vestibular schwannoma may compress the trigeminal nerve and cause loss of the corneal reflex

The trigeminal root lies just above the cerebellopontine angle. As a vestibular schwannoma enlarges upward it compresses V, and loss of the corneal reflex is often the first sign of trigeminal involvement.
The facial nerve, though stretched, often keeps function surprisingly well, so facial weakness is a late sign.
The glossopharyngeal nerve lies above the trigeminal nerve

IX lies below VII and VIII, with X and XI, heading for the jugular foramen. V lies above, heading for Meckel's cave.
From above down at the angle: V, then VII and VIII, then IX, X and XI. A large tumour can reach both groups.
